<reason>CON built a competent case (unresolved germline safety, rarity/opportunity cost, slope) and later sharpened it into "public money buys relatedness, not health," plus a non-identity point about MRT creating a different child. But PRO seized on CON's own clipped opening ("private access under license") and never let go: if the risks justified refusal, CON would demand a ban, not a bill, so the real dispute is a means test. CON's "we license experimental drugs but don't fund them" analogy was clever but imperfect, since CON's plan is private-pay clinical provision, not a sponsored trial, and PRO's charge that the state collects registry data while families carry bill and risk went unanswered. PRO also answered both pressure questions directly and credibly (program cost rides on existing donor-egg IVF infrastructure; restriction is in the motion's own words "to prevent severe inherited mitochondrial disease," undercutting CON's smuggling charge), and turned CON's "preference" argument back on the already-funded donor-egg IVF precedent. CON's threshold answer was reasonable but retreated from its "fifty years" opening framing. Both sides argued well; PRO made the decision cleaner.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's B2.1–B2.2 and closing B5.1–B5.3: "safe enough to license, too dangerous to fund" is not a safety position but a means test on avoiding a fatal disease. CON's formulary analogy (A2.1, A5.1) was a real answer but did not neutralize the equity charge that the same children would be born privately under CON's own plan.</best_rebuttal>
